# Pi Bot
**An open-source, local-first AI agent team for your desktop.** Named AI Bots work on your own
computer: chat with one or put several in a group chat, and they plan, run commands, edit files,
browse the web and use your computer, while every risky step waits for your approval. Runs on
macOS, Windows and Linux, with an Android app. Built on the [pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi)
agent kernel.
 ▶  Watch the 60-second video  ·  Download  ·  User guide  ·  Online docs  
[English](README.md) · [中文](README.zh-CN.md) · [日本語](README.ja.md)
Pi Bot is a desktop app in which a team of named Bots works on your own computer. You chat with a
Bot directly or put several in a group chat, give them a working folder, and they plan, run
commands, edit files and hand work to each other, while every risky step waits for your approval.
The "brain" runs on your machine too: chats, files, memory and keys stay local, and only the
model provider you choose sees the prompts you send.

itens.descricao_en: Long-term memory runtime for AI agents — plain Markdown as the source of truth, local ranked retrieval, and an independent sleep-time Manage layer. Claude Code and Codex share one store. No API key.
itens.readme:
### agent-memory: the long-term memory runtime for AI agents
 Invariants  ·  Skill  ·  Issues 
***
An agent that closes its session forgets everything it learned in it. agent-memory is the
runtime that fixes that, for any agent — not only coding ones. Markdown files in one store are
the single source of truth, the SQLite index beside them is a cache you can delete at any time,
and Claude Code, Codex CLI, Muse Code, and anything else that can run a shell command share
that store.
Retrieval is local and ranked, and it answers with paths rather than pasted text — the agent
opens each hit only as deep as the task needs. Writes do not wait for the agent to remember to
make them: they fire at conversation boundaries. A sleep-time pass then consolidates and
forgets by value, on its own clock. None of it needs an API key.
## Two lines, one store
Agent memory has grown along two architectural lines. One builds a **retrieval engine** —
embeddings, a knowledge graph, a ranking pipeline — which finds the right thing, but hands the
agent an opaque chunk it cannot inspect and a store it cannot migrate off. The other hands the
agent a **filesystem** — markdown it reads directly, browsable with `ls` and `grep` — which is
legible and costs nothing to run, but does not rank, and stops scaling the moment the tree
outgrows a listing.

**LoopForge** is a self-hosted workspace where your team ships software with coding agents. Describe what you need to **Main Bot** in chat: it opens a Docker sandbox, checks out your repositories, delegates to project roles, and opens the PR. When a way of working proves itself, save it as an **SOP** (a standard workflow of agents, scripts and human gates) so the next requirement is delivered the same way, with review and approval built in.
Coding-agent CLIs do the work: CodeBuddy, Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Cursor CLI, Antigravity, Kimi Code, Pi, DeepSeek Harness and ZCode. LoopForge adds the roles, sandboxes, checkpoints and history around them, all on your own infrastructure under the MIT license.
## Two ways to work
| | **Chat with Main Bot** | **Run an SOP** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Best for | Exploring, quick fixes, iterating with the agent | Repeatable delivery with fixed stages and sign-off |

# Skill Recorder
**Record yourself doing a task once, then turn it into a skill your AI agent can repeat.**
> [!TIP]
> **Want to install Skill Recorder? [Go to the latest release](https://github.com/microsoft/skill-recorder/releases/latest).**
> Scroll to **Commit-pinned installation** and copy the complete command for your
> operating system. It is ready to paste: you do not need to edit it or download
> the source code yourself. [Step-by-step instructions below](#install-it).
Skill Recorder captures a real work session on your screen: the clicks, the app and
window switches, the pages you visit, commands/output from its optional recorded terminal,
and (if you want) your spoken narration. It then uses
the **GitHub Copilot CLI** to reconstruct *what you actually did* as a clear **intent plus
an ordered list of steps**. From there, one step turns that single run into something an
agent can reuse:
- a **Skill**: a `SKILL.md` procedure an agent runs on demand, or
- an **Automation**: the same procedure on a schedule or trigger.
Both prefer the agent's **native tools** (like the `gh` CLI or `web_fetch`) over replaying
UI clicks, and generalize from your one example, so recording yourself submitting *one*
form can teach the agent to submit *all* of them.

1. 🔴 **Record.** Hit record (or `⌘⇧R` / `Ctrl+Shift+R` from anywhere) and just do your
